rv.q: This punchy revival doesn't need the nostalgic assist and makes a strong case for the play as both a major work of its time and a tart commentary still very much with us.

Burr — perhaps the least expected to shine on theater’s biggest stage — almost steals the show, perfect for the volcanic Dave Moss, a twitchy ball of fury unleashing f-bombs at a machine-gun rate, which seems in synch with Burr’s diatribes about modern culture. He turns out to be the most comfortable with Mamet’s tricky dialogue.

In the right hands, and this production is in nothing if not right hands, Glengarry Glen Ross unfolds brilliantly, as pure and elegant a demonstration of modern theater as has been pieced together in many decades.
This new production is simply the latest modern contextualization of Mamet’s masterpiece, or a belated anniversary gift.
Mr. Mamet’s savage comedy may be his finest achievement, along with “American Buffalo,” which deals with similar themes and similarly desperate men.
Dialed to a slightly lower register, the delicacy and intricacy of the language here lands with a punch whose impact comes on the subway ride home.
And so a finely made blade has become a blunter object.
Culkin, though, has a staccato delivery, a halting rhythm and an innate sense of vulnerability, all qualities that have made him a much-cherished star.
Because it is so tautly and distinctively written, and since most of the actors are good, Glengarry Glen Ross still basically works; it still hooks you in.
But the casual racism, which rings off-key more than 40 years later, underlines a question already hanging over the whole show: What are we doing here?
The starry revival currently at the Palace Theatre offers a refresher — though not necessarily deep feelings of purpose or clarity.
It’s Mamet, so the “f–k”s still fly.
But in the weirdly limp revival that opened on Monday at the Palace Theater, something has flipped.
“Glengarry” still crackles with vicious energy, bitter humor, and brutal truths about American ambition.
With a dynamite cast firing on all cylinders, these “Glengarry” leads are ultimately worth the investment.

Odenkirk makes this crushing failure visceral: the initial desperation, the fleeting joy, the catastrophic fall—a performance of extraordinary architecture and energy that lifts the role to classic stature.
Glengarry, which feels painfully small in the vast theater, still packs a punch, thanks to Mamet's beautifully crafted dialogue.
That misstep aside, the production remains highly entertaining.

With such an impressive list of actors, audiences will likely flock to Glengarry Glen Ross simply because they want to see Odenkirk, Burr, McKean, and Culkin knock it out of the park — and that is what they will find in spades.
The good news is that, aside from one questionable casting decision, David Mamet's brackish masterpiece is in solid hands in Patrick Marber's production.

Their mouths shoot dirty words like buckshot, their competitiveness makes European soccer hooligans look like sissies, their verbiage is as oily as an Oklahoma gusher, and their desperation is only centimeters from turning criminal. They and what they do, it would seem, need a large yellow warning label: TOXIC.
Thanks to its better performances, this “Glengarry Glen Ross,” if not as sizzling as fans might have hoped, doesn’t disappoint accordingly.
And if there’s a good reason to revive Glengarry Glen Ross again, and Mamet’s cavernously amoral depiction of immorality inside it, Marber hasn’t made that apparent either.

That's what's missing, the requisite team play that would prepare the field so one or more of the otherwise excellent actors might hit one out of the park instead of merely participating in a game of catch.

Beamed into 2025—via the enduring cultural imprint of the 1992 movie starring Al Pacino and Alec Baldwin—this revival of Glengarry Glen Ross, starring Kieran Culkin, Bob Odenkirk, Bill Burr, and Michael McKean, lands with a puzzling, bitter thud.
Polished, starry, and with nothing to say, this Glengarry sells a McMansion, neither a scam nor a Palace.
But this new Glengarry never quite makes a successful pitch for its bill of goods.
This Glengarry Glen Ross has no sense of urgency, place, or purpose.

Given the high prices the production is asking for tickets, the inconsistency of the acting, and the unwise choice of using a less-than-intimate theater, I feel those who spend their money on this “Glengarry Glen Ross” are getting an even rawer deal than the show’s characters.

A normal review struck me as almost irrelevant when I saw audience members take obvious delight at the foul-mouthed, hateful, racist invective of Mamet’s characters, laughing at the ugliest lines. It suddenly made me think of “House of Games,” a film that Mamet wrote a few years after he got his Pulitzer.
If you have disposable income and can stomach the characters’ racism and ageism, the top-notch cast delivers Mamet in his prime.
That is to say that under Patrick Marber’s direction, it is overwrought, overacted and implausible.

cn.t: Critics are mixed on this star-studded revival, with most praising the performances (especially Odenkirk and Burr) but questioning whether Mamet's play needs another Broadway outing so soon, finding the production competent but lacking urgency.

sg.ra: After the 2023 TSX lift the orchestra received wider seats and a slight rake, and center rows G-K are the unobstructed sweet spot before the mezzanine overhang begins at Row K per the official chart; AVFMS reports suggest the overhang only becomes visually noticeable closer to Row N-O, so center G-K is the cleanest post-reno picture.

sg.vl: Discount seats but mezz starts to bite
sg.ra: The mezzanine overhang begins cutting in roughly at Orchestra Row K per the theatre's official seating chart, so rear-orchestra tickets (Row N onward) are priced well below center-premium but you give up the top of the proscenium; one AVFMS reviewer at Row N seat 119 still reported no overhang intrusion, so the rear orch is a real value play on non-spectacle shows that don't use high flying scenery.

Post-2023 lift reviewers specifically call out that the front-mezz sightline is 'incredible' and gives a panoramic view of the choreography, and multiple sources name center Rows A-C (or middle C-F) as the unobstructed sweet spot; avoid the first two side-aisle seats in Row A which Broadway Direct flags as obstructed by a safety railing that survived the renovation.

Unlike most Broadway houses, the Palace rear mezz sits on the same elevated tier rather than under a balcony overhang, so sightlines stay open to the top of the proscenium even at the back — a November 2025 AVFMS reviewer confirmed you are 'pretty high up but atleast you have a full view of the stage'; the tradeoff is distance plus the tight 1920s row spacing the reno preserved.

The Palace's mezz-level boxes are routinely sold as obstructed-view and nytix explicitly warns 'the box seats are not recommended, as they do not provide a clear view of the stage' — the severe side angle means upstage-left blocking is cut off; pick them only if you want the close-in vibe over actually seeing the full stage picture, and never for a dance-heavy or spectacle title.

The balcony survived the lift essentially unchanged — nytix flags that 'the view from the first row of the balcony may be blocked by a large horizontal bar, so sitting in the rows behind the first row is recommended,' and post-reno reviewers still call the balcony 'pretty far' from stage; there is no step-free access, so even the cheapest seat carries real friction.
